goal: The intrusive narrator aims to render the Christmas Eve city as a living social organism — warmth, community, and festive abundance spreading across every class — so that Scrooge's refusal of the carol singer lands as deliberate self-exile rather than mere eccentricity.

goal: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come's implicit goal is to show Scrooge the human consequence of his death — specifically, that his existence caused harm rather than good, and that his dying has produced relief rather than grief.

goal: Scrooge is trying to maintain his rational disbelief — to dismiss what his senses are reporting as humbug and protect his settled, skeptic's peace of mind
conflict: The ghost itself, which does not argue or threaten but simply arrives — passing through a locked door, appearing with incontrovertible physical specificity, radiating cold; reality refuses to cooperate with Scrooge's interpretation of it
crisis: Scrooge cannot disbelieve what he is seeing and feeling without contradicting his own senses, yet belief means accepting that everything he has built his worldview on — rational materialism, the dismissal of superstition — is wrong
decision: Scrooge chooses to keep fighting his own senses — he looks the phantom through and through, marks its every detail, and still refuses to ratify what he perceives; defiance becomes the decision because capitulation is unthinkable

goal: The narrator's goal is to establish Marley's death as absolute, irrefutable fact before the story proper begins — to make the reader incapable of doubting it.
conflict: The claim "Marley was dead" is inherently vulnerable to readerly skepticism, since the story is about to produce his ghost; the narrator must preemptively close every avenue of doubt while acknowledging the absurdity of the very simile he relies on.
crisis: The narrator must simultaneously convince the reader that Marley is dead and hold the reader's affection — too solemn and the argument becomes tedious; too playful and the death loses weight.
decision: The narrator chooses conspiratorial humor as the vehicle for absolute conviction: he jokes about the door-nail, admits he cannot defend it, defers to ancestral wisdom anyway, and repeats the claim more emphatically than before — performing certainty through comic self-interruption rather than in spite of it.
key_actions: Narrator asserts Marley's death and lists the witnesses who signed the burial register; narrator cites Scrooge himself as signatory and vouches for Scrooge's financial credibility as warrant for the signature's authority; narrator digresses on the door-nail simile, admits uncertainty about it, and defers to ancestral wisdom rather than abandoning the phrase; narrator repeats the death claim emphatically after the digression; narrator explains that Scrooge continued doing business on the day of Marley's funeral and got a good bargain; narrator invokes Hamlet's father as precedent for why a ghost requires a certified dead man behind it; narrator notes Scrooge never painted out Marley's name and answered to both names indifferently; narrator delivers the satirical portrait of Scrooge as a cold, hard, solitary miser whose internal freeze manifests physically; narrator describes the social void around Scrooge — no greetings, no beggars, no children, even blind men's dogs pulling their owners into doorways; narrator reports that Scrooge actively liked this isolation.
key_dialogue: "MARLEY was dead: to begin with. There is no doubt whatever about that."; "Mind! I don't mean to say that I know, of my own knowledge, what there is particularly dead about a door-nail."; "my unhallowed hands shall not disturb it, or the Country's done for"; "This must be distinctly understood, or nothing wonderful can come of the story I am going to relate."; "If we were not perfectly convinced that Hamlet's Father died before the play began, there would be nothing more remarkable in his taking a stroll at night, in an easterly wind, upon his own ramparts, than there would be in any other middle-aged gentleman rashly turning out after dark in a breezy spot"; "No eye at all is better than an evil eye, dark master!"; "To edge his way along the crowded paths of life, warning all human sympathy to keep its distance, was what the knowing ones call 'nuts' to Scrooge."
emotions: conspiratorial playfulness as the narrator invites the reader into the joke about the door-nail; mock-solemnity as the narrator defers to ancestral wisdom and threatens national ruin; dry amusement as the narrator notes Scrooge solemnised the funeral with an undoubted bargain; wry intellectual complicity as the Hamlet comparison is offered; mild unease as Scrooge's indifference to Marley's name begins to shade the comedy; gathering coldness as the physical portrait of Scrooge accumulates adjective by adjective; desolation as the social void around Scrooge is rendered — no greetings, no beggars, no children, dogs pulling away; bleak finality as Scrooge is revealed to actively relish the isolation.
motifs: the door-nail — a piece of ironmongery invoked and immediately questioned, its deadness undefended but enforced by collective wisdom; Scrooge's signature on the burial register — his name as financial instrument, creditworthiness standing in for moral weight; Marley's name above the warehouse door, unpainted-out, years after death — the dead partner still present in the firm's identity; flint and oyster — hard, cold, sealed things from which nothing generous emerges; the cold Scrooge carries inside him

goal: Scrooge has no goal of his own — he is a passive observer, compelled by the Spirit to witness; his implicit goal is to understand what the Spirit is showing him
conflict: The scene offers no object of sympathy or moral foothold — the men are strangers to grief, and the dead man is unnamed; Scrooge cannot locate himself in what he sees
crisis: Scrooge cannot ask the question the scene forces on him — whose funeral is being laughed about — and cannot look away from the answer gathering around him
decision: Scrooge turns to the Spirit for explanation rather than confronting what he already suspects
key_actions: The Spirit and Scrooge arrive at the Royal Exchange without transition — the city springs up around them; the Spirit stops beside a knot of businessmen and points; Scrooge advances to listen; the men discuss an unnamed dead man with yawns and a snuff-box and a shaking nose-excreescence; the conversation turns to his money, then to a cheap funeral, then to the joke of volunteering to attend only if lunch is provided; the most disinterested speaker declares he was probably the dead man's most particular friend because they used to stop and speak when they met; the group disperses into other clusters; Scrooge looks to the Spirit for explanation
key_dialogue: "No, I don't know much about it, either way. I only know he's dead."; "I thought he'd never die."; "God knows," said the first, with a yawn.; "What has he done with his money?"; "He hasn't left it to me. That's all I know."; "It's likely to be a very cheap funeral, for upon my life I don't know of anybody to go to it. Suppose we make up a party and volunteer?"; "I don't mind going if a lunch is provided. But I must be fed, if I make one."; "When I come to think of it, I'm not at all sure that I wasn't his most particular friend; for we used to stop and speak whenever we met."
emotions: detached observation (Scrooge watches the familiar Exchange as he always has); unease (the Spirit's pointed hand singles out this group); suspended comprehension (the dead man is unnamed; the death is abstract); growing chill (the yawning indifference accumulates — no one cares, no one mourns); unspoken recognition beginning to press at the edges (Scrooge knows these men; the description fits); bewilderment turning toward dread (he looks to the Spirit and receives no answer)
motifs: money in pockets, chinked and counted — the sound of commerce as the only language these men speak; watches consulted and gold seals trifled with — time and status as the sole currencies of attention; the snuff-box, vast and performative — appetite displayed where feeling should be; the pendulous nose-excreescence shaking like a turkey-cock's gill — the body as grotesque, appetite made flesh; yawning, repeated — boredom as the true response to death among men who traded only in self-interest; the laugh, twice noted — collective merriment at what should be grief; black gloves never worn, lunch always required — the comedy of a friendship measured in coats and meals
subtext: The speaker claims intimate friendship because they spoke when they met; don't state that this is Scrooge's own social arithmetic returned to him

goal: No clear volitional goal — Scrooge enters as an invisible, passive witness; his only implicit aim is to endure the crossing and observe
conflict: The warmth and belonging of Fred's household press against Scrooge's defenses — he cannot argue, intervene, or dismiss what he sees; he can only feel it
crisis: The scene offers no action-choice for Scrooge; the crisis is internal — he must either hold his contempt or admit that what Fred's household has is precisely what his own choices have cost him
decision: Scrooge surrenders to the experience — he guesses aloud at the parlor games as if he belongs there, and begs the Spirit for more time like a child; the posture of detachment collapses

He believed it too!"; "More shame for him, Fred!"; "He's a comical old fellow — that's the truth: and not so pleasant as he might be. emotions: detached unease (crossing the dark abyss); abrupt surprise at the laugh and the bright room; involuntary pleasure at the laughter spreading through the party; a pang at hearing Fred defend him without anger; softening at the harp tune and its connection to the boarding-school child; helpless delight in the parlor games; a complicated sting when he hears himself described as a disagreeable, growling animal; unexpected warmth at the toast — gratitude and longing simultaneously; grief at being swept away before the feeling resolves
motifs: the dark abyss and moaning wind, giving way without transition to a bright lamplit room; Fred's laugh — full-bodied, contagious, impossible to resist; the firelight and dessert clustered around it as the scene's visual and social center; the harp tune — a simple air that links the present party to the child at the boarding-school; the toast of mulled wine raised to a man not present
subtext: Fred says Scrooge loses pleasant companions by his own choice; don't say that Fred's unconditional warmth is the thing Scrooge cannot argue away

goal: Fred wants to persuade Scrooge to join his Christmas dinner and soften toward human fellowship
conflict: Scrooge's philosophically entrenched contempt for Christmas and human connection, defended with economic argument and withering dismissal
crisis: Fred cannot counter Scrooge's cynicism with logic — he can only offer warmth against a man who has armored himself against warmth; continuing costs him dignity, leaving costs him hope
decision: Fred chooses to leave without anger, repeating his Christmas wishes to the end and bestowing them on Cratchit as he goes
key_actions: Fred enters flushed and glowing from rapid walking in the cold; Scrooge attacks Christmas with economic logic; Fred counters Scrooge's "you're poor" with "you're rich enough — what reason have you to be morose"; Scrooge delivers his boiled-with-his-own-pudding tirade; Fred gives his "fellow-passengers to the grave" speech; Cratchit involuntarily applauds then pokes the fire to extinguish the last spark; Scrooge threatens Cratchit with dismissal and mocks Fred as a parliamentarian; Fred invites Scrooge to dinner; Scrooge refuses with the full expression about where Fred can go; Fred presses "why" and Scrooge deflects with "why did you get married"; Scrooge repeats "Good afternoon" four times as Fred tries further appeals; Fred leaves without anger and wishes Cratchit a merry Christmas; Scrooge mutters about retiring to Bedlam
key_dialogue: "Merry Christmas! What right have you to be merry? What reason have you to be merry? You're poor enough."; "Come, then — what right have you to be dismal? What reason have you to be morose? You're rich enough."; "every idiot who goes about with 'Merry Christmas' on his lips, should be boiled with his own pudding, and buried with a stake of holly through his heart"; "the only time I know of, in the long calendar of the year, when men and women seem by one consent to open their shut-up hearts freely, and to think of people below them as if they really were fellow-passengers to the grave"; "I want nothing from you; I ask nothing of you; why cannot we be friends?"; "Good afternoon!" goal: To be ready — to pull back his own curtains, position himself at watch, and challenge the Second Spirit the moment it appears rather than being seized by surprise
conflict: The Spirit does not appear on cue; instead, a sourceless blaze of ruddy light fills the room with no shape attached to it, which is precisely the category of strangeness Scrooge's preparations could not anticipate
crisis: A best bad choice between two forms of helplessness — remain in bed paralyzed by inexplicable light, or get up and move toward the unknown without any assurance of what he will find
decision: He gets up softly, shuffles to the door in his slippers, and puts his hand on the lock — choosing to move toward the mystery rather than wait for it to come to him
key_actions: Wakes mid-snore and orients himself to the hour without being told; pulls back all his own bed-curtains with his own hands; lies down and establishes a watch all around the bed; the bell strikes one and no shape appears; suffers a violent fit of trembling; lies motionless at the center of a blaze of ruddy light for a quarter of an hour; gradually begins to reason that the light may come from the adjoining room; gets up softly and shuffles in his slippers to the door; puts his hand on the lock; hears a strange voice call his name and bid him enter; obeys
key_dialogue: "a strange voice called him by his name, and bade him enter"
emotions: Wary self-possession and deliberate readiness; confidence in his own preparedness; trembling dread as the minutes pass with no apparition; helpless, suspended alarm at the sourceless light; tentative reasoning reasserting itself; cautious, self-directed resolve as he rises and moves; abrupt surrender of initiative at the voice
motifs: The bell striking one — the supernatural appointment kept as pure sound before any shape arrives; the bed-curtains pulled back by Scrooge's own hands — the same gesture that was done to him in Stave II, now reversed; the blaze of ruddy light with no source or shape — presence without form, more alarming than a ghost because it cannot be faced; the slippers — the shuffling, domestic, undignified means by which he moves toward the unknown; the hand on the lock — the threshold moment, agency at its limit before it is overridden
subtext: Scrooge pulls back the curtains himself and takes up a watching position to challenge the Spirit, but the gestures perform courage rather than embody it; don't state this

goal: Scrooge wants to buy the prize turkey and have it delivered anonymously to Bob Cratchit's house before Christmas morning.
conflict: No internal opposition — the conflict is comic: the body won't cooperate (shaking hand, inability to stop laughing), and the sheer scale of the turkey creates a logistical problem.
crisis: None of the conventional dramatic kind — the crisis is comic and physical: Scrooge's joy is so total it is almost incapacitating, and the turkey is so large it cannot be carried.
decision: Scrooge pays for a cab without hesitation; he writes the address with a shaking hand anyway; he insists on anonymity.
key_actions: Scrooge leans out the window and interrogates a boy about the prize turkey; Scrooge sends the boy to buy the turkey, promising escalating payment for speed; Scrooge whispers his plan to send it to Bob Cratchit anonymously while rubbing his hands and laughing; Scrooge writes the delivery address with a shaking hand; Scrooge opens the street door to wait and notices the door knocker; Scrooge pats the knocker and exclaims over it; the turkey arrives and Scrooge declares it too large to carry; Scrooge pays for the turkey, the cab, and the boy — chuckling through each payment; Scrooge sits down breathless and laughs until he cries; Scrooge shaves while his hand shakes, dancing; Scrooge dresses in his best and goes out into the streets; strangers wish him Merry Christmas and he receives it as the greatest sound he has ever heard.

Go and buy it"; "Come back with him in less than five minutes and I'll give you half-a-crown!"; "I'll send it to Bob Cratchit's! He sha'n't know who sends it. It's twice the size of Tiny Tim. Joe Miller never made such a joke as sending it to Bob's will be!"; "I shall love it, as long as I live! I scarcely ever looked at it before. What an honest expression it has in its face! It's a wonderful knocker!"; "Here's the Turkey! Hallo! Whoop! How are you! Merry Christmas!"; "Why, it's impossible to carry that to Camden Town. You must have a cab."
emotions: barely-contained hilarity at the boy's slang skepticism; gleeful conspiratorial secrecy in whispering the plan; physical abandon as laughter overtakes him; tender wonder at the door knocker; pure open-armed delight at the turkey's arrival; breathless exhausted joy after paying; unguarded happiness on the streets; something close to reverence receiving the strangers' Christmas greetings.
motifs: the prize turkey — enormous, ridiculous, almost alive in its absurdity, too large for any practical use; the door knocker — the same object that showed Marley's face, now patted like an old friend; the shaking hand — the body registering what the will has decided; the boy off like a shot — velocity as joy; chuckle repeated four times across a single sentence, accumulating like a drumroll.

goal: Maintain denial — dismiss the apparition as a hallucination or indigestion and avoid confronting what it means for himself
conflict: Marley's ghost, whose physical reality keeps breaking through Scrooge's rationalizations — the moving hair in still air, the dropped jaw, the chain's noise — and whose message implicates Scrooge directly
crisis: Irreconcilable goods — if the ghost is real, Scrooge must accept that his own life has been building an identical chain; if it is not real, he must explain away evidence his senses cannot dismiss
decision: Scrooge abandons denial, falls to his knees, and accepts the ghost's reality and authority — then tries to manage the terms of the haunting rather than resist it
key_actions: Scrooge meets the ghost with cold caustic questions; asks whether the ghost can sit, watching it anxiously; deploys the undigested-beef speech as a deflection; waves a toothpick to redirect the ghost's stare; holds the chair as the ghost screams and shakes its chain; falls to his knees when the jaw drops; remains on his knees with hands in pockets as he questions Marley about the chain; tries to negotiate the three spirits into one visit; watches the ghost rebind its jaw and disappear
key_dialogue: "There's more of gravy than of grave about you, whatever you are!"; "I wear the chain I forged in life. I made it link by link, and yard by yard; I girded it on of my own free will, and of my own free will I wore it. Is its pattern strange to you?"; "Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence, were, all, my business."; "I--I think I'd rather not"; "Couldn't I take 'em all at once, and have it over, Jacob?"
emotions: cold contemptuous scepticism; anxious practical caution (the chair question); performed bravado masking rising terror; escalating physical fear (marrow disturbed, needing to grip the chair); complete collapse into submission and trembling; wary, humbled curiosity about the chain; business-like composure reasserting itself even on his knees; dismay at the prospect of three spirits; deflated resignation
motifs: the chain — forged link by link through personal choice, worn across Marley's body, clanked and flung to the floor; the dropped jaw and its bandage — removed and replaced, marking the scene's turn from scepticism to submission; the moving hair and tassels agitated in still air — the ghost's own atmosphere; Scrooge's hands in his breeches pockets — a habitual gesture of self-possession that persists even while kneeling; the fireplace, the chair opposite — domestic furniture made uncanny

goal: Scrooge wants to escape the presence of the shrouded corpse — to leave the dead man's bedchamber and end his exposure to what the Phantom is showing him.
conflict: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come refuses to move, its finger fixed immovably on the covered head; and Scrooge finds he physically cannot lift the sheet himself, trapped between compulsion and paralysis.
crisis: Best bad choice — Scrooge can try to uncover the face and know for certain whose body this is, or he can refuse to look and remain suspended in dread; neither option offers relief, and both lead toward the same unbearable knowledge.
decision: Scrooge chooses not to lift the sheet — he acknowledges the impulse, admits the physical ease of it, but cannot bring himself to act; he then abandons the attempt to leave and instead begs the Spirit to show him someone who grieves for this man, seeking any evidence that the dead man's life was not entirely without human connection.
key_actions: Scrooge recoils from the bed as the scene changes around him; glances around the dark room in anxious inspection; looks toward the Phantom and sees its finger pointing at the covered head; considers and fails to lift the sheet; hears no voice but registers words when he looks at the body; observes the empty house — no mourner, no kind word left behind; hears a cat at the door and rats gnawing beneath the hearth-stone; attempts to persuade the Spirit to leave; is refused and held by the pointing finger; confesses he lacks the power to uncover the face; begs to be shown anyone in the town who feels emotion at this death
key_dialogue: "Spirit! this is a fearful place. In leaving it, I shall not leave its lesson, trust me. Let us go!"; "I understand you, and I would do it, if I could. But I have not the power, Spirit. I have not the power."; "If there is any person in the town, who feels emotion caused by this man's death, show that person to me, Spirit, I beseech you!"
emotions: Shock and physical recoil on entering the changed scene; anxious, compulsive scrutiny of the dark room; dread and paralysis before the uncoverable face; a suspended, unvoiced grief (the words heard only in looking at the body); mounting desolation at the image of total abandonment; revulsion at the cat and the rats; desperate urgency in the plea to leave; helpless shame at confessing powerlessness; agonised, suppliant dread in the final beseechment
motifs: The bare, uncurtained bed — stripped of comfort and dignity; the ragged sheet covering the body — a veil that announces rather than conceals; the Phantom's unmoved, pointing finger — authority that will not relent; the pale light falling only on the bed — illumination without warmth; the plundered, bereft, unwatched quality of the room — absence rendered as physical texture; the cat at the door and the rats beneath the hearth-stone — creatures drawn to death, restless in the dark
subtext: Scrooge pleads to leave and then to see a mourner; don't state he already suspects whose body this is.

goal: Scrooge's goal entering the scene is to close the counting-house and surrender as little as possible — specifically, to deny or minimize the Christmas Day holiday without open confrontation.
conflict: The established custom of Christmas Day wages for no work — an implicit social contract Cratchit expects honored and Scrooge cannot refuse outright without appearing monstrous even by his own standards.
crisis: Scrooge cannot refuse the holiday without a social rupture he is unwilling to cause, yet granting it freely violates his core conviction that money paid without labor is money stolen; he must choose between open tyranny and grudging capitulation.
decision: Scrooge grants the day but reframes it as theft and conditions it on Cratchit's early return, converting surrender into a kind of punishment.
key_actions: Scrooge dismounts from his stool with visible ill-will; Cratchit snuffs his candle and puts on his hat the instant the hour arrives; Scrooge demands to know whether Cratchit wants the full day; Scrooge buttons his great-coat to the chin while delivering his complaint; Scrooge walks out with a growl; Cratchit closes the office in an instant; Cratchit goes down a slide on Cornhill twenty times with a lane of boys; Cratchit runs home to Camden Town as hard as he can.

If I was to stop half-a-crown for it, you'd think yourself ill-used, I'll be bound?"; "And yet, you don't think me ill-used, when I pay a day's wages for no work."; "A poor excuse for picking a man's pocket every twenty-fifth of December! But I suppose you must have the whole day. Be here all the earlier next morning."
emotions: Scrooge's sour, effortful resentment as he dismounts and admits the hour; Cratchit's restrained, watchful anticipation; Scrooge's aggrieved self-pity as he frames the holiday as robbery; Cratchit's careful, minimal responses — faint smile, brief observation — neither provoking nor capitulating; Scrooge's bad-tempered resignation as he grants the day on his own terms and growls out; Cratchit's sudden, uncontained physical joy the moment Scrooge is gone.
motifs: The snuffed candle — extinguished the instant permission is implicitly granted; the great-coat buttoned to the chin against cold Scrooge refuses to acknowledge in others; the white comforter with dangling ends in place of the great-coat Cratchit does not own; the slide on Cornhill repeated twenty times — pure, effortful, purposeless pleasure; the boys forming a lane for the slide; running as hard as he could pelt toward Camden Town.
subtext: Scrooge delivers his grudging permission as a moral lecture on theft; don't state that the lecture is self-indictment.

goal: Maintain total control over his property, his time, and his warmth — to sit in his counting-house on Christmas Eve and conduct business without any leak of resource, sentiment, or heat
conflict: The cold itself, which presses against every chink and keyhole; the implicit social expectation of Christmas generosity; and Bob Cratchit's physical suffering, which is a constant visible demand on Scrooge's coal-box
crisis: The coal-box sits in Scrooge's room; every time Cratchit needs warmth, Scrooge must choose between relenting or threatening dismissal — a choice that arrives not once but as a standing rule
decision: Scrooge keeps the coal-box in his own room and makes explicit that the clerk reaching for the shovel will mean their parting — converting a potential act of generosity into a structural impossibility

emotions: Settled, self-sufficient authority (Scrooge at his desk, absorbed, requiring nothing from the world); the world's cold pressing in without touching him; a faint grotesque absurdity accumulating as the reader watches Cratchit fail to warm himself at a candle
motifs: Fog pouring through every chink and keyhole, obscuring the houses opposite into mere phantoms; candles flaring in neighboring windows like ruddy smears on brown air; Cratchit's fire reduced to one coal; Cratchit's white comforter; Cratchit trying and failing to warm himself at a candle flame; Scrooge's door held open not for welcome but for surveillance
subtext: Scrooge keeps the door open and calls the threatened dismissal a practical prediction; don't state that the open door is a control mechanism and the threat is the only warmth he offers

goal: Scrooge tries to determine whether Christmas Day has passed — whether his chance to act on the transformation he has undergone still exists
conflict: He has no direct knowledge of the date; the night with the Spirits collapsed time so completely that he genuinely cannot orient himself

goal: Approach the charity collector he humiliated the day before and make amends with a large donation

goal: Scrooge has no active goal entering this scene — he is a passenger, carried by the Ghost into a past he did not choose to revisit

goal: Settle into his chambers, reassure himself, and restore ordinary domestic routine after the uncanny event at the door-knocker
conflict: The involuntary apparition of Marley's face, which erupts from every tile on the fireplace and refuses to be suppressed by rational will
crisis: Whether to acknowledge that what he is experiencing is genuine dread or to dismiss it again as imagination and press on with his evening as if nothing has happened
decision: He chooses defiant denial — speaks the word aloud and crosses the room, asserting willed rationalism over involuntary fear
key_actions: double-locks the door (departing from his custom); removes his cravat and changes into nightclothes; sits before a near-dead fire and tends it for warmth; scans the Dutch tiles on the fireplace, each bearing a scriptural figure; sees Marley's face displace every figure on every tile; speaks aloud and crosses the room

emotions: effortful composure (securing the room, changing clothes, settling to routine); uneasy concentration (coaxing warmth from a meagre fire); momentary absorption in the tiles' figures; involuntary dread as Marley's face swallows all other images; forcible, defiant override — the spoken denial reasserting control
motifs: the double-lock (departure from custom as physical evidence of fear beneath the "humbug"); the dying fire on a bitter night (warmth effortfully extracted, comfort minimal and grudging); the Dutch tiles crowded with scriptural figures — Cains, Abels, Pharaoh's daughters, Apostles — each a story about consequence and judgment; Marley's face rising through every tile like a rod swallowing all else; the single spoken word as incantation against fear

goal: Scrooge wants to cross the threshold of Fred's house and be received as a welcome guest — to enter the life he previously refused.
conflict: His own nerve fails him — he cannot bring himself to knock; the niece startles at his sudden appearance, momentarily registering the intrusion of someone who does not belong.
crisis: To knock or not knock — each pass of the door is a small version of the same irreconcilable choice: the man he was (who rejected this house) against the man he is trying to be (who belongs in it).
decision: He makes a dash and knocks; then, without waiting to be led, puts his hand on the dining-room lock and lets himself in.

emotions: Nervous exhilaration on the morning streets; mounting suspense at the door through a dozen passes; a sudden surge of resolve; brief alarm at startling the niece; naked vulnerability in the announcement "It's I"; unconditional welcome flooding in as Fred seizes him; expansive, almost wordless joy as the whole party gathers.
motifs: The door as threshold crossed and recrossed before the final dash; the dining-room table spread for the feast Scrooge once refused; Scrooge's face sidling around the door — half in, half out — before he commits; the niece in the corner with a footstool, an intimate domestic detail that marks how fully Scrooge has forgotten this household; the narrator's breathless stutter — "won-der-ful happiness!" — breaking into syllables as language strains against the feeling.

goal: Survive the night without supernatural visitation — to wait out the promised hour and have nothing happen, so he can dismiss Marley's ghost as a dream
conflict: The clock itself refuses to cooperate with his scepticism (it strikes twelve when it should be two); his own mind springs back to Marley every time he tries to reason the ghost away; and the Spirit arrives exactly as promised, making denial impossible
crisis: A best-bad-choice with no good option: surrender to the supernatural claim on him (which means accepting that his life requires reclamation) or resist (which means falling from the window as a mortal man)
decision: He rises and goes with the Spirit — not from courage or willingness, but because the gentle grasp cannot be resisted and the hand on his heart promises he will not fall
key_actions: wakes in total darkness and cannot tell window from wall; checks the church bell, which strikes twelve when it should be past two; verifies with his own repeater watch, which also strikes twelve; gets out of bed and rubs frost from the window to confirm it is still night; returns to bed and cannot stop thinking about whether Marley's ghost was a dream; resolves to stay awake until one o'clock strikes; counts each quarter-chime aloud; speaks his triumph a beat too early, before the hour bell sounds; light floods the room and the bed-curtains are drawn aside by a hand; finds himself face to face with the Spirit, which fluctuates between forms; asks the Spirit's identity and purpose; begs the Spirit to put on its cap; is told the cap is made of his own passions; the Spirit seizes him gently by the arm and commands him to rise and walk; Scrooge clutches the Spirit's robe in fear of falling; the Spirit lays its hand on his heart and promises he will be upheld

Take heed!"; "Rise! and walk with me!"; "I am a mortal and liable to fall."; "Bear but a touch of my hand there, and you shall be upheld in more than this!"
emotions: groggy disorientation shading into alarm at the wrong hour; frantic scepticism (the clock must be broken; the sun must have failed); relief when the window confirms it is still night; compulsive, circular thought about whether Marley was real; resolved dread — he sets himself to wait out the hour; mounting tension counted off in quarter-chimes; premature triumph (he speaks too soon); shock as light floods and the curtains are drawn; wary awe at the Spirit's paradoxical appearance; practical embarrassment redirected into bureaucratic questioning; involuntary reverence when rebuked about the cap; faint dry protest about the inconvenience of the visit; helpless surrender as the gentle grasp proves irresistible; naked fear at the window; something that is not yet hope but is the precondition for it — the hand on the heart
motifs: the clock and its chimes — each quarter sounded aloud, time refusing to be mastered or dismissed; darkness and the difficulty of seeing — frost on the window, ferret eyes piercing nothing, light arriving only with the Spirit; the bed-curtains drawn aside by a hand — the intimate domestic space invaded from within, not without; the Spirit's fluctuating form — a child and an old man at once, dissolving and re-forming, one arm then twenty legs then none; the jet of light from the Spirit's crown and the extinguisher cap held under its arm; the holly branch paired with summer flowers — winter and summer occupying the same hand; the gentle grasp that cannot be resisted

goal: Scrooge has no goal entering this scene — he wakes without agenda, and the scene's energy comes from discovering that he is free to want things again
conflict: Nothing directly opposes Scrooge; the conflict is internal and residual — disorientation, disbelief, the body's shock at feelings it has been starved of for decades

goal: Scrooge's goal entering this scene is to complete his evening routine — dinner, newspapers, banker's-book — and return home to bed without incident or interruption.
conflict: The house itself resists the affectlessness of the routine; the physical character of the chambers — the darkness of the yard, the fog and frost at the gateway — refuses to be ignored, pressing in on Scrooge's ordinary movement with something that feels like waiting.
crisis: Not a conscious dilemma for Scrooge, but the structural irony the scene turns on: a man who has reduced his life to pure routine must pass through a place the narrator frames as supernaturally alert — the scene asks whether the familiar can still ambush him.
decision: Scrooge gropes through the dark yard with his hands and enters — no hesitation, no acknowledgment of anything unusual. The routine holds.

motifs: the repeated "melancholy" applied to both dinner and tavern, doubling until the word becomes texture rather than description; the chambers once belonging to his deceased partner, Marley's absence present in the ownership of the rooms; the dark yard where even Scrooge's long familiarity fails him and he must use his hands; the black old gateway wreathed in fog and frost; the Genius of the Weather as a personified presence, mournful and still, occupying the threshold between outside and in

goal: The intrusive narrator has no concrete objective; the POV is observational — the scene's functional goal belongs to the Ghost of Christmas Present, who aims to show Scrooge that Christmas abundance flows from human spirit and that Sabbatarian legislation done in his name is a betrayal of that spirit
conflict: Scrooge's attempt to catch the Spirit in a contradiction — accusing him of supporting the very Sunday trading restrictions that deny the poor their one festive day — poses the central opposition; the Spirit must distinguish authentic generosity from the cruelty enacted in its name
crisis: Scrooge has cornered the Spirit with a genuine logical trap: if Sabbatarian laws are enacted in the name of Christmas, then the Spirit of Christmas Present is either complicit in denying the poor their dinners or must disavow the institutions that claim to represent him — an irreconcilable goods between institutional religion and authentic generosity
decision: The Spirit disavows those who do cruelty in his name — "who are as strange to us and all our kith and kin, as if they had never lived" — and instructs Scrooge to charge those deeds on the perpetrators themselves; Scrooge promises to do so

goal: Scrooge has no conscious objective entering this scene — he is being transported rather than acting; his operative goal is to maintain composure and emotional distance from whatever the Ghost shows him
conflict: The landscape of his childhood triggers involuntary physical and emotional responses that bypass his defenses entirely — grief surfaces before he can suppress or rationalize it
crisis: Irreconcilable goods — he can protect his defended self by denying what he feels (as he tries to do, attributing tears to a pimple), or he can let the feeling be real, which means confronting the boy he abandoned
decision: Scrooge chooses to stop defending; he does not correct the Ghost's leading question about the solitary child — he says he knew it, and sobs

goal: Scrooge has no goal entering this scene — the Ghost acts without warning; Scrooge is a passenger, not a pursuer
conflict: The evidence the Ghost forces Scrooge to witness contradicts the rationalization Scrooge has built his life on — that warmth and generosity are privileges of comfort, not universal human impulses

goal: Scrooge has no goal entering this scene — he is a passive observer, compelled to witness by the Ghost, not pursuing an objective of his own.
conflict: The scene's opposition is not external resistance to a goal but the confrontation between Scrooge's self-protective detachment and the meaning the Ghost is forcing him to see; he cannot look away, cannot intervene, and cannot deny what the thieves' logic mirrors back at him.
crisis: Scrooge must either accept that the isolated, despised dead man is himself — that his present course leads here — or find some way to disavow the connection and preserve his self-conception.
decision: He does not disavow; he names the connection aloud to the Ghost, acknowledging that the dead man's life and end are the trajectory of his own.
